concepts.title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: We use parameterized functions to represent continuous radiance fields by recording a finite set of parameters that define a function giving field values at any coordinate.
concepts.content:
Continuous fields have infinite resolution, so we cannot explicitly represent them by recording values at all possible positions. Instead, we use parameterized functions to represent continuous fields. These functions take any continuous position as input and output the field's value at that location. This approach is called an implicit representation because we do not explicitly store the field values at all coordinates; rather, we record a finite set of parameters of a function that can provide the field value at any coordinate. Implicit representations are also used in variational autoencoders (VAEs), where an infinite set (an infinite mixture of Gaussians) is represented via a parameterized function from a continuous input domain. You can consider a VAE as a continuous field mapping from latent variables to images.

Many different parameterized functions $L_{\theta}$ can represent our target radiance field $L$. For example, we could use a neural network (e.g., @mildenhall2020nerf), a mixture of Gaussians (e.g., @kerbl20233d), or other function approximators. The key property is that the field $L_{\theta}$ is differentiable with respect to the parameters $\theta$, enabling gradient-based optimization to find parameters that yield a desirable field (used when fitting a radiance field to images). Whatever function family we use, it takes input coordinates and produces colors and densities as output (@fig-nerfs-nerf_module). Because these functions are differentiable, we can view them as modules in a differentiable computation graph (@fig-nerfs-nerf_module). Later, multiple such modules are combined and optimized via backpropagation to fit the field to a set of images.
concepts.motivation_md: Continuous radiance fields have infinite resolution, making explicit storage impossible; parameterized functions provide a finite, differentiable way to represent and optimize these fields.
concepts.recap_md:
- Continuous fields can't be explicitly stored at all positions, so parameterized functions represent them implicitly.
- Parameterized functions take coordinates as input and output field values.
- Differentiable parameterizations enable gradient-based optimization to fit radiance fields to images.

concepts.title: Positional encoding for NeRFs

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Fourier positional encodings help NeRFs model high-frequency variations abundant in radiance fields.
concepts.content:
NeRF includes a positional encoding layer to transform the raw coordinates into a Fourier representation. It uses the same positional encoding scheme as transformers (see @sec-transformers-positional_encodings). @fig-nerfs-flatland_positional_encoding shows how this scheme translates the $XY$-coordinate field of Flatland to positional encodings:

(see figure: The first layer of NeRF applies positional encoding to the input coordinate values. Here we show the resulting positional codes for all possible input coordinate values $(X,Y)$ within some range.)

Fourier positional encodings are very effective for NeRFs because they help the network model high-frequency variations, which are abundant in radiance fields @tancik2020fourier. Why do such encodings help model high frequencies? Essentially, in regular Cartesian coordinates, the location $(0,0)$ is much closer to $(1,1)$ than to $(100,100)$, but this isn't necessarily the case with Fourier positional codes. Because of this, with Cartesian coordinates as inputs, an MLP will be biased to assign similar values to $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ and different values to $(0,0)$ and $(100,100)$. Conversely, with Fourier positional codes as input, this bias is reduced. This makes it easier for the MLP, taking Fourier positional codes as input, to fit high-frequency functions that change rapidly, such as assigning very different output values to $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$. See @tancik2020fourier for a more thorough analysis of this phenomenon.
concepts.motivation_md: Fourier positional encodings reduce bias in neural networks, enabling them to fit high-frequency details in radiance fields more effectively.

- This helps model high-frequency variations in radiance fields.
- Fourier codes reduce bias present with Cartesian inputs, aiding MLP fitting.

concepts.title: Other Ways of Parameterizing Radiance fields

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Radiance fields can be parameterized by differentiable functions other than neural nets, such as voxel-based representations or mixtures of Gaussians.
concepts.content: In principle, $L_{\theta}$ could be other kinds of functions, including those that are not neural networks. The important property is that it be differentiable so we can optimize its parameters to fit a given scene. One alternative is to parameterize radiance fields using a voxel-based representation, as explored in, e.g., @fridovich2022plenoxels. Another alternative is to use a mixture of Gaussians @kerbl20233d. In this case, each Gaussian represents a semi-transparent ellipsoid of some color $\mathbf{c}$ and some density $\sigma$. When many such Gaussians overlap, their sum can approximate scene content very well.
concepts.motivation_md: Exploring alternative differentiable parameterizations of radiance fields allows for different trade-offs in representation and optimization.
concepts.recap_md:
- Radiance fields can be parameterized by differentiable functions beyond neural nets.
- Voxel-based representations are one alternative.
- Mixtures of Gaussians represent scene content via overlapping ellipsoids.

concepts.title: volume rendering

position.section_title: Rendering Radiance Fields

concepts.one_liner: Volume rendering computes images from radiance fields by integrating radiance values along camera rays weighted by density.
concepts.content:
We use volume rendering to render images from radiance fields, as methods like NeRFs do, though other rendering methods are possible. Volume rendering works by integrating the radiance values along each camera ray. Imagine looking into a hazy volume of colored dust: the integral sums all color values along the ray, weighted by a value related to the dust's density. A cartoon visualization is given in @fig-nerfs-flatland_volume_rendering, and real rendering results are shown in @fig-nerfs-flatland_training. The volume rendering equation is:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \ell(r) = \int_{t_n}^{t_f}\alpha(t) \, \overbrace{L^\sigma(r(t))}^{\text{density}} \, \overbrace{L^c(r(t),\mathbf{D})}^{\text{color}} \, dt\\
    \alpha(t) = \exp \Big(-\int_{t_n}^{t} \underbrace{L^\sigma(r(t))}_{\text{density}} dt\Big)
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Volume rendering integrates radiance and density along rays to produce realistic images from radiance fields.
concepts.recap_md:
- Volume rendering integrates radiance values along camera rays.
- The integral weights colors by density, like looking through hazy colored dust.
- This method is used by NeRFs to render images from radiance fields.

concepts.title: plenoptic function

position.section_title: Introduction

concepts.one_liner: The plenoptic function fully describes all light rays traveling through space by their position, direction, wavelength, and time.
concepts.content: The plenoptic function tries to answer the question: "What information about the world is contained in the light filling a region of space?" Given a scene, the plenoptic function is a full description of all the light rays that travel across the space (@fig-nerfs-plenoptic_function). It tells us the light intensity of a light ray passing through the three-dimensional (3D) point $(X, Y, Z)$ from the direction given by the angles $(\psi, \phi)$, with wavelength $\lambda$, at time $t$: $$L(X, Y, Z, \psi, \phi, \lambda, t)$$ In this chapter we will ignore time and use only three color channels instead of the continuous wavelength. We can represent the plenoptic function with the parametric form $L_{\theta}$ where the parameters $\theta$ have to be adapted to represent each scene.
concepts.motivation_md: The plenoptic function exists to comprehensively represent all light information in a scene, enabling understanding and reconstruction of visual data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Plenoptic function describes all light rays in space.
- Depends on position, direction, wavelength, and time.
- Often simplified by ignoring time and using RGB channels.

concepts.title: vector fields

position.section_title: What is a Radiance Field?

concepts.one_liner: Vector fields assign a vector to each position in space and are a general way to represent functions varying over space.
concepts.content:
Radiance fields are an example of vector fields, which are functions that assign a vector to each position in space. For example, we might have a vector field $f: X, Y, Z \rightarrow v_1, v_2$, where $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are coordinates and $v_1$ and $v_2$ are some values. Let's take a moment to consider field-based representations more broadly, since they turn out to be a very important way of representing scenes. Essentially, fields are a way to represent functions that vary over space, and fields appear all over the place in this book. For example, every image is a field: it is a mapping from pixel coordinates to color values. The images we usually deal with in computer vision are discrete fields (the input coordinates are discrete-valued) but in this chapter we will instead deal with continuous fields (the input coordinates are continuous-valued). Unlike regular images, fields can also be more than two-dimensional and can even be defined over non-Euclidean geometries like the surface of a sphere. Because they are such a general-purpose object, fields are used as a scene representation in many contexts. Some examples are the following:

-   **Pixel** images, $f: x, y \rightarrow r, g, b$, are fields with the property that the input domain is discrete, or, equivalently, the field is piecewise constant over little squares that tile the space.

-   **Voxel** fields, $f: X,Y,Z \rightarrow \mathbf{v}$ are discrete fields that can represent values $\mathbf{v}$ like spatial occupancy, flux, or color in a volume. They are like 3D pixels. Like pixels, they have the special property that they are piecewise constant over cubes the size of their resolution.

-   **Optical flow fields**, $f: x, y, t \rightarrow u, v$, measure motion in a video in terms of how scene content flows across the image plane. We encountered these fields in @sec-3D_motion_and_its_2D_projection.

-   **Signed distance functions** (**SDFs**) @curless1996volumetric, $f: X,Y,Z \rightarrow d$, represent the distance to the closest surface to point $[X,Y,Z]^\mathsf{T}$. This is a useful representation of geometry.
    
Notation reminder: we use capital letters for world
concepts.motivation_md: Vector fields provide a flexible and general framework to represent spatially varying quantities, useful across many computer vision and graphics tasks.

- Vector fields assign vectors to spatial positions.
- Fields can be discrete or continuous and vary in dimensionality.
- Examples include pixel images, voxel fields, optical flow, and signed distance functions.

concepts.title: Benefits of Volume Rendering for Optimization

position.section_title: Fitting a Radiance Field to Explain a Scene

concepts.one_liner: With volume rendering, small changes to the scene content yield small changes to our loss; that is, we have small but non-zero gradients, enabling gradient-based optimization.
concepts.content: After around 2,500 steps of gradient descent, we have arrived at a fairly accurate representation of the scene. At this point, the objects' densities are high enough that volume rendering essentially amounts to just ray casting (finding the color of the first surface we hit). So why did we use volume rendering? Not because we care about volumetric effects; in this scene there are none. Rather, it makes it possible for optimization to find the ray casting solution. With volume rendering, small changes to the scene content yield small changes to our loss; that is, we have small but non-zero gradients. Ray casting, in contrast, is an all-or-none operation, and therefore small changes to scene content can yield drastic changes to the rendered images (an occluder can suddenly hide the object that was previously in view of a pixel). This makes gradient-based optimization difficult with ray casting, but achievable with volume rendering. concepts.title: the rendering equation

position.section_title: Beyond Radiance Fields: The Rendering Equation

concepts.one_liner: The rendering equation models light scattering off surfaces by summing emitted light and light scattered from all other surface points.
concepts.content:
Fortunately, other, more general rendering models exist that better handle multi-bounce effects. Perhaps the most general is the rendering equation, introduced by Kajiya @Kajiya1986 in computer graphics. The goal was to introduce a new formalism for image rendering by directly modeling the light scattering off the surfaces composing a scene. The rendering equation can be written as,

$$L(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = g(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') \left[ e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') + \int_S \rho(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}',\mathbf{x}^{\prime\prime}) L(\mathbf{x}',\mathbf{x}^{\prime\prime}) d\mathbf{x}^{\prime\prime} \right]
$$

where $L(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')$ is the intensity of the light ray passing from point $\mathbf{x}'$ to $\mathbf{x}$ (analogous to the plenoptic function but with a different parameterization). The function $e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')$ is the light emitted from $\mathbf{x}'$ to $\mathbf{x}$ and represents light sources. The function $\rho(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}',\mathbf{x}^{\prime\prime})$ is the intensity of light scattered from $\mathbf{x}^{\prime\prime}$ to $\mathbf{x}$ by a surface patch at location $\mathbf{x}'$ (related to the bidirectional reflectance distribution function).

Here $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{x}'$, and $\mathbf{x}^{\prime\prime}$ represent vectors of world coordinates, e.g., $\mathbf{x} = [X,Y,Z]$.

The term $g(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')$ is a visibility function encoding the scene geometry and occlusions. If points $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{x}'$ are not visible to each other, the function is 0; otherwise, it is $1/\lVert \mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}' \rVert ^2$, modeling how energy propagates from each point.

In Kajiya's words, "The equation states that the transport intensity of light from one surface point to another is simply the sum of the emitted light and the total light intensity which is scattered toward $\mathbf{x}$ from all other surface points." Integrating this equation can be done using numeric methods and has been the focus of numerous studies in computer graphics.

While this rendering model is more powerful than the one radiance fields use, it is also more costly to compute. In the future, as hardware improves, we may see a movement away from radiance fields toward models that more fully approximate the full rendering equation.

- It includes visibility and scattering functions to represent scene geometry and surface properties.
- More powerful but computationally costly than radiance fields, it may guide future rendering advances.

position.section_title: Concluding Remarks

concepts.one_liner: Radiance fields aim to model the full plenoptic function, building on multiview geometry, signal processing, and neural networks.
concepts.content: Radiance fields try to model the light content in a scene. The ultimate goal is to model the full plenoptic function, that is, all physical properties of all the photons in the scene. Along the way to this goal, many simplified models have been proposed, and radiance fields are just one of them. Methods for modeling and rendering radiance fields build upon many of the topics we have seen earlier in this book, such as multiview geometry, signal processing, and neural networks. They appear near the end of this book because they rest upon almost all the foundations we have by now built up.

concepts.title: ray casting

position.section_title: Rendering Radiance Fields

concepts.one_liner: If the particle density is infinite, the ray terminates at the surface of the object, reducing volume rendering to measuring the color of the first surface hit by each ray exiting the camera.
concepts.content: If the particle density is zero, then we have free space, which contributes nothing to the integral. If the particle density is infinite, we have a solid object, and after the ray intersects such an object, $\alpha$ immediately goes to zero and the ray essentially terminates at the surface of the object. Putting these two cases together, if we have a scene with solid objects and otherwise empty space, *then volume rendering reduces to measuring the color of the first surface hit by each ray exiting the camera*. This simple model, called **ray casting**, is in fact how many basic renderers work, such as in the standard rasterization pipeline @shirley2009fundamentals.

- Infinite particle density causes rays to terminate at object surfaces.
- Ray casting measures the color of the first surface hit by each camera ray.

concepts.title: Computing the Volume Rendering Integral

position.section_title: Rendering Radiance Fields

concepts.one_liner: The volume rendering integral has no simple analytical form and must be approximated numerically, often using a quadrature rule that sums weighted samples along a ray.
concepts.content:
The volume rendering integral has no simple analytical form. It depends on the function $L$, which may be arbitrarily complex; think about how complex this function will have to be to represent all the objects around you, including their geometry, colors, and material properties. Because of this, we must use numerical methods to approximate @eq-nerfs-vol_rendering_integral.

One way to do this is to approximate the integral as a discrete sum. A particularly effective approximation is the following, which is called a quadrature rule (see  @max1995optical, @max2005local for justification of this choice of approximation): 

$$\begin{aligned}    \ell(r) &\approx \sum_{i=1}^T \alpha_i \, (1-e^{-L^\sigma(\mathbf{R}_i)\delta_i}) \, L^c(\mathbf{R}_i, \mathbf{D})\\
    &\alpha_i = \exp\Big(-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} L^\sigma(\mathbf{R}_j)\delta_j\Big)\\
    &\delta_i = t_{i+1} - t_i
\end{aligned}$$ where we have now replaced our continuous radiance field from @eq-nerfs-vol_rendering_integral with a discrete vector of samples from the radiance field, $\{\mathbf{R}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{R}_T\}$, where $\mathbf{R}_t = r(t)$ is the world coordinate of a point distance $t$ along the ray $r$.

@fig-nerfs-flatland_volume_rendering visualizes this procedure:

(see figure: Volume rendering of our Flatland radiance field.)

Here we have a 2D radiance field of our Flatland scene, and we are looking at it from above. We show how two cameras (gray triangles in corners) view this scene. The camera sensors are depicted as a row of five pixels, indexed by coordinate $x$. We send a ray outward from the camera origin through each pixel to query the scene. Each ray gets sampled at the points that are drawn as circles. The size of the circle indicates the $\alpha$ value and the color/transparency of the circle indicates the color/density of the radiance field at that point. In this scene, we have solid objects, so the density is infinite within the objects and as soon as a ray hits an object, all remaining points become occluded from view ($\alpha$ goes to zero for the remaining points, as indicated by the circles shrinking in size).

In this figure, we took samples at evenly spaced increments along the ray. Instead, as suggested in @mildenhall2020nerf, we can do better by chopping the ray into $T$ evenly spaced intervals, then sampling one point at uniform within each of these intervals. The effect of this is that all continuous coordinates will get sampled with some probability, and therefore if we run the approximation over and over again (like we will when using it in an optimization loop; see @sec-nerfs-nerf_section) we will eventually take into account every point in the continuous space (they will all be supervised during fitting a radiance field to explain a scene).

Following this strategy, for a ray whose origin is $\mathbf{O}$ and whose direction is $\mathbf{D}$, we compute sampled coordinates $\{\mathbf{R}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{R}_T\}$ as follows: 

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{R}_i &= \mathbf{O} + t_i\mathbf{D}\\
    &t_i \sim \mathcal{U}[i-1,i]*\frac{t_f-t_n}{T}+t_n
\end{aligned}$$

- Samples along the ray are weighted by transmittance and density to compute color.
- Sampling points uniformly within intervals ensures coverage of the continuous space during optimization.

concepts.title: Rendering pipeline for radiance fields

concepts.one_liner: The rendering pipeline maps pixel coordinates to colors by computing rays, sampling points along them, and applying volume rendering.
concepts.content:
Our task is to compute the image $\boldsymbol\ell$ that will be seen by a specified camera viewing the scene. We need to find the color of each pixel in this image. To find the color of a pixel, $\boldsymbol\ell[n,m,:]$, at camera coordinate $n,m$, the first step is to find the ray (origin $\mathbf{O}$ and direction $\mathbf{D}$) that passes through this pixel. This can be done using the methods we have encountered in this book for modeling camera optics and geometry, which we will not repeat here (see @sec-pixel_to_rays. The key pieces of information we need to solve this task are the camera origin, $\mathbf{O}_{\texttt{cam}}$, and the camera matrix, $\mathbf{K}_{\texttt{cam}}$, that describes the mapping between pixel coordinates and world coordinates (steps for constructing $\mathbf{K}_{\texttt{cam}}$ are given in @sec-simple_system_revisited-adapting_the_output). We apply this mapping, then compute the unit vector from the origin to the pixel to get the direction $\mathbf{D}$ (@fig-nerfs-pixel2ray):


(see figure: Module for mapping from pixel coordinates to the world coordinates of a ray through that pixel.)

In this chapter, we represent RGB images as $N \times M \times 3$ dimensional arrays.


Next we sample world coordinates along the ray, as described previously (@fig-nerfs-ray2coords):


(see figure: Module for sampling coordinates along a ray.)

Finally, we use the volume rendering integral (using the quadrature rule approximation given previously) to compute the color of the pixel (@fig-nerfs-vrender):


(see figure: Module for volume rendering of a single ray.)

This pipeline gives a mapping from pixel coordinates to color values: $n,m \rightarrow r,g,b$. Our task in the next section will be to explain a set of images as being the result of volume rendering of a radiance field, that is, we want to infer the radiance field from the photos.

- Compute the ray origin $\mathbf{O}$ and direction $\mathbf{D}$ for each pixel.
- Sample points along the ray to query the radiance field.
- Apply volume rendering integral to compute pixel color from samples.

Our task is to compute the image $\boldsymbol\ell$ that will be seen by a specified camera viewing the scene. We need to find the color of each pixel in this image. To find the color of a pixel, $\boldsymbol\ell[n,m,:]$, at camera coordinate $n,m$, the first step is to find the ray (origin $\mathbf{O}$ and direction $\mathbf{D}$) that passes through this pixel. This can be done using the methods we have encountered in this book for modeling camera optics and geometry, which we will not repeat here (see @sec-pixel_to_rays. The key pieces of information we need to solve this task are the camera origin, $\mathbf{O}_{\texttt{cam}}$, and the camera matrix, $\mathbf{K}_{\texttt{cam}}$, that describes the mapping between pixel coordinates and world coordinates (steps for constructing $\mathbf{K}_{\texttt{cam}}$ are given in @sec-simple_system_revisited-adapting_the_output). We apply this mapping, then compute the unit vector from the origin to the pixel to get the direction $\mathbf{D}$ (@fig-nerfs-pixel2ray):


(see figure: Module for mapping from pixel coordinates to the world coordinates of a ray through that pixel.)

In this chapter, we represent RGB images as $N \times M \times 3$ dimensional arrays.


Next we sample world coordinates along the ray, as described previously (@fig-nerfs-ray2coords):


(see figure: Module for sampling coordinates along a ray.)

Finally, we use the volume rendering integral (using the quadrature rule approximation given previously) to compute the color of the pixel (@fig-nerfs-vrender):


(see figure: Module for volume rendering of a single ray.)

concepts.content:
## Fitting a Radiance Field to Explain a Scene {#sec-nerfs-fitting}

In this section our goal is to find a radiance field that can explain a set of observed images. This is the task our denizens of Flatland have to solve as they walk around their world and try to come up with a representation of the scene they are seeing. This is the task of vision. Rendering radiance fields into images (view synthesis) is a graphics problem. We are now moving on to the vision problem, which the inverse problem and is where we really wanted to get: inferring the radiance field that renders to an observed set of images.

Concretely, our task is to take as input a set of images, along with the camera parameters for the cameras that captured those images. We will produce a parameterized radiance field as output. The full fitting procedure therefore maps $\{\boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}, \mathbf{K}^{(i)}_{\texttt{cam}}, \mathbf{O}^{(i)}_{\texttt{cam}}\}_{i=1}^N \rightarrow L_{\theta}$.

Our objective is that if we render that radiance field, using each of the input cameras, the rendering will match the input images as closely as possible.
